information.content: Time-dependent beta-lactam antibiotic used for susceptible Gram-positive, some Gram-negative and anaerobic infections. Route and species are especially important in small herbivores.
Do not give oral penicillins to rabbits, and do not administer penicillins by any route to guinea pigs, chinchillas, hamsters, gerbils or degus unless specialist-directed.
Macrolide antibiotic used for selected respiratory, chlamydial, mycoplasmal, Helicobacter and intracellular infections where culture/clinical evidence supports use.
Avoid or reduce/use carefully in renal or hepatic impairment and be mindful of drug interactions with methylxanthines, steroids and digoxin.
Monobactam antibiotic with Gram-negative activity, included here for fish bacterial infection protocols.
EMA category A Avoid. Reserve for exceptional, justified cases where other options are unsuitable and susceptibility supports use.
First-generation cephalosporin with Gram-positive and selected Gram-negative activity. Time-dependent, so dosing interval and compliance matter.
Avoid oral administration in small herbivores such as rabbits; GI dysbiosis/enterotoxaemia risk is clinically important.
Third-generation cephalosporin used for serious Gram-negative infection or sepsis-type cases where stewardship supports escalation.
Reserved use. Avoid oral administration in small herbivores and monitor renal risk if used with nephrotoxic drugs.
Long-acting third-generation cephalosporin used for selected prolonged-treatment infections, but the long half-life is not consistent across exotics.
Do not use in rabbits, guinea pigs or other small herbivores. Avoid pregnancy/lactation and use stewardship restraint.
Third-generation cephalosporin with active metabolite, used in serious susceptible infections where a higher-tier beta-lactam is justified.

pearls.pearl: With penicillins in exotics, the route can be the cliff edge. Rabbit oral penicillin is not a small mistake.
Azithromycin is often chosen for awkward intracellular infections, but it still needs stewardship reins, not confetti dosing.
Aztreonam is not a casual aquarium sprinkle. Treat it like the locked cupboard antibiotic it is.
Cefalexin is time-dependent: missed doses let the bacteria sneak through the portcullis.
Third-generation cephalosporins are escalation tools, not the first screwdriver pulled from the drawer.
Convenia is not conveniently long-acting in every species. Exotics enjoy ruining assumptions.
Ceftiofur intervals are wonderfully species-weird: a cockatiel and a python do not read the same clock.
Cefuroxime has a place, but the evidence map in exotics is more candlelight than floodlight.
Ciprofloxacin has range, but range is not permission to fire wildly.
Clarithromycin is an interaction octopus. Check the tentacles before combining it.
Clindamycin and rabbits belong in separate rooms with a locked door between them.
Oxytetracycline in water is chemistry as well as medicine. If the tank turns sinister brown, act.
